1.pericope_label: Therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God, Of the doctrine of baptisms, and of laying on of hands, and of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment. And this will we do, if God permit.

schools.summary: Correct the received rendering to the doctrine of the first principles, give the margin's literal sense as the word of the beginning, and prefer let us press onwards, since there is an urgency the ordinary rendering misses; note that the word for perfection answers to the one rendered full grown just before and expresses maturity of growth. On the plural baptisms, consider and reject the rendering baptisms of teaching, on the ground that teaching would be the point of resemblance between the Jewish and Christian rites rather than the point of contrast, and explain the presence of the word doctrine as guarding against the impression that the repetition of a rite is meant. Or settle it by authority: the plural by itself never means specifically Christian baptism either here or elsewhere but ablutions such as the mystery religions and the Jewish cultus required of initiates, proselytes and worshippers. Admit that the laying on of hands seems out of place among elementary principles, and list the occasions on which it served as a sign — of blessing, of healing, in the choice of the Seven, in the bestowal of the Spirit, in separation for a task, in ordination — noting that prayer accompanied it. On the closing qualification, insist it is no idle form but a real condition: the writer means that he will go on with the argument and not attempt to lay the foundation again.

Turn the exhortation on a builder's image. By first principles understand the rudiments taught to the ignorant when they are received into the church, and insist that leaving them does not mean forgetting them but not remaining in them; for in building a house the foundation is never left, yet to be always engaged in laying it would be ridiculous, since whoever never proceeds to the superstructure wearies himself with useless labour. Then read the two middle clauses as a parenthesis in apposition to the rest, since otherwise there would be the absurdity of repetition — for what is the doctrine of baptism but faith, repentance and judgment, already named? Reject the account of the plural that makes it refer to a first baptism abrogated by returning to first principles, and take it instead of the solemn rites or the stated days of baptizing. Then hear in the closing qualification a dreadful denunciation rather than a pious formula: there ought to be no delay, for there will not always be opportunity for making progress, and it is not in man's power to bound at once from the starting point to the goal, progress in the course being the special gift of God. On the plural, canvass at length the change of number, the different persons and times, the threefold immersion, the threefold baptism of spirit, blood and water, and the inward set beside the outward — then judge none of them solid, since there is but one baptism, and settle on the divers washings among the Jews.

Turn the rebuke on the present congregation. You have heard how much the apostle found fault with the Hebrews for wishing to be always learning the same things, and with good reason, since when for the time they ought to have been teachers they needed someone to teach them the elements again; and the same might fitly be said of you, who do not even maintain the rank of learners but, ever hearing the same things on the same subjects, are in the condition of those who hear no one at all. Add what the loss costs the teacher: oftentimes when he wishes to go on further and touch on higher and more mysterious themes, the want of attention in those who are to be taught prevents him.

Quote a great predecessor at length and then decline to follow him. Give the argument in full — that doctrine is itself called baptism, that John's baptism was his doctrine and Christ's the doctrine wherewith he should sprinkle many nations, so that the two gospel baptisms are its teaching and the gifts of the Spirit, the latter being what the laying on of hands intends — and then say plainly that, with all this great man's learning, he has not hit the apostle's meaning, since teaching is the means by which the gifts are obtained and the apostle never designed to separate them. Read the opening word as pointing back to their indolence and slowness of heart, and gloss leaving the principles as ceasing to continue in the state of babes who must be fed with milk.

sides.position: Because two are taught, by water and by the Holy Ghost, the first an emblem of the second
Because the divers washings among the Jews are meant; none of the usual explanations of the plural is solid, since there is but one baptism
Because the plural by itself never means specifically Christian baptism, but ablutions such as the mystery religions and the Jewish cultus required
Because the solemn rites, or the stated days of baptizing, are meant; the clause is a parenthesis in apposition to the rest
Because the two gospel baptisms are its teaching and the gifts of the Spirit — an argument quoted from Owen and then rejected

debates.question: Should it be rendered baptisms of teaching?

sides.position: No: teaching would be the point of resemblance between the Jewish and Christian rites, not the point of contrast
The word doctrine is there to guard against the impression that the repetition of a rite is meant

debates.question: What force has if God permit?

sides.position: A simple recognition of dependence, as in any undertaking however pleasing to God
No idle form but a real condition: he means he will go on with the argument and not lay the foundation again
A dreadful denunciation: there will not always be opportunity, and progress in the course is the special gift of God

outliers.note: Alone sets out a predecessor’s argument in full and then rejects it by name, saying that with all Owen’s learning he has not hit the apostle’s meaning, since teaching is the means by which the Spirit’s gifts are obtained and the two were never meant to be separated.

Alone turns the rebuke on his own congregation, telling them the same charge might fitly be made of them, and adding that a teacher who wishes to go on to higher themes is prevented by the inattention of those he teaches.

themes: leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ
let us go on unto perfection

4.pericope_label: For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost, And have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come, If they shall fall away, to renew them again unto repentance; seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame.

schools.summary: Take the described experiences at face value: they are all actual spiritual experiences, and the adverb means once for all rather than once upon a time. Add that the language about tasting the good word cannot be applied to an impenitent sinner, who has no relish for the truth and sees no beauty in it, so that only a true Christian can be said to taste and enjoy it. Reorganise the clauses grammatically, so that enlightened is not the first term of a series but the thing the following clauses explain. On the disputed participle, agree that the ordinary translation is altogether incorrect, the Greek admitting one rendering only — but reject the charge of dogmatic bias against the translators, since tracing the version back finds it due not to the Genevan versions but to Erasmus, Luther and Tyndale. Or concede on the authority of another that there is no if in the Greek while defending the common version as not improperly expressing the sense, treating the whole as a supposed case that may never occur. Then refuse to soften the verdict: the infinitive with that adjective bluntly denies the possibility of renewal for apostates, it is a terrible picture which cannot be toned down, and the one ray of light comes later and not here. Correct the familiar rendering of the reason, since the prefix in the verb for crucifying does not mean again or afresh but up.

Approach the word impossible through its history of abuse. The passage led many to repudiate the epistle, because the Novatians armed themselves with it to deny pardon to the fallen, and the Western churches refused its authority rather than refute them. Then reject two evasions offered by its defenders: that impossible means rare or difficult, which is wholly different from its meaning, and that the repentance meant is only the discipline preparing catechumens for baptism, since to deny that an appendage of baptism could be repeated would carry no weight against the secure and the wavering. Defend the severity as just, since the man suffers only the punishment of his own defection, and this is not inconsistent with the mercy offered to sinners as soon as they sigh for it, because repentance is required which one wholly fallen from the gospel never truly feels; such are deprived of the Spirit and given up to a reprobate mind, ceasing not to add sin to sin until, wholly hardened, they either fear nothing or curse the judge they cannot escape. Alternatively, hold that the case cannot be supposed of true believers at all, who may fall into affliction and even into sin and lose the lively exercise of grace, but not irrecoverably, being held by a threefold cord of Father, Son and Spirit.

Narrow the reference sharply before explaining any term: the words have no reference to any person professing Christianity, do not belong to backsliders of any kind, and apply only to apostates who reject the whole Christian system and join the blaspheming Jews in calling Christ an impostor and vindicating his murderers. Then take the conditional apart. Quote the argument that the earlier participles are aorists properly rendered in past time, so that this one should have been too, but that the translators followed Beza, who without authority from any ancient manuscript inserted the word if, that the text might not appear to contradict the perseverance of the saints — and add that the man who made this objection was himself a Calvinist, a thorough scholar who consulted candour rather than his creed. Or say more bluntly still that here is not a supposition but a plain relation of fact, describing those who have cast away both the power and the form of godliness, and that of these wilful total apostates it is declared impossible to renew them again, though they were renewed once.

debates.question: Who is described in the warning?

sides.position: Not any professing Christian and not backsliders of any kind, but apostates who reject the whole system and join the blaspheming Jews
Apostates from Christ; the experiences named are all actual spiritual experiences and the picture cannot be toned down
Those who have cast away both the power and the form of godliness, wilfully and totally
The case cannot be supposed of true believers, who may fall but not irrecoverably, being held by a threefold cord

debates.question: Is if they shall fall away a defensible rendering?

sides.position: No: the aorist requires have fallen away, and the if was inserted by Beza without manuscript authority to protect the perseverance of the saints
The rendering is certainly wrong, but the charge of dogmatic bias is unfounded — it goes back not to the Genevan versions but to Erasmus, Luther and Tyndale
There is no if in the Greek, yet the common version is not improper: a supposed case is meant, which may never in fact occur
Here is not a supposition but a plain relation of fact
Not rare or difficult, which is wholly different from its meaning; nor confined to the discipline preparing catechumens for baptism
It bluntly denies the possibility of renewal for apostates; the one ray of light comes later and not here

outliers.note: Alone defends the translators against the charge of dogmatic bias while agreeing the rendering is wrong, tracing the conditional back past the Genevan versions to Erasmus, Luther and Tyndale.

Alone approaches the word impossible through its history of abuse, recalling that the Novatians armed themselves with the passage to deny pardon to the fallen and that Western churches refused the epistle’s authority rather than refute them.

themes: crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh

7.pericope_label: For the earth which drinketh in the rain that cometh oft upon it, and bringeth forth herbs meet for them by whom it is dressed, receiveth blessing from God: But that which beareth thorns and briers is rejected, and is nigh unto cursing; whose end is to be burned.

schools.summary: Sharpen the picture climatically: land which not only receives but drinks in abundant rain must, in the climate in view, either bring forth herbage or be condemned as irretrievably barren, and the clause about tilling is added precisely to show that nothing was wanting on the part of the owner or of those who worked it. Correct two renderings, giving for whom it is also tilled rather than by whom it is dressed, and taking the blessing received as a share in what God pronounces on the fruitful earth. Note that the word for herbs is a green plant from the verb to feed, and that drinking in distinguishes mellow soil from rock where the rain runs off. On the burning, say the allusion is to the common practice among Oriental and Roman farmers of burning bad and barren lands, and cite Pliny for it — or look instead to the description of the land God overthrew, which is brimstone and salt and burning, adding the botanical detail that the presence of caltrops is sure evidence of a poor soil on which labour will be wasted, and noting that the phrase is partly a quotation from the curse in Genesis. Supply the military note that Roman soldiers scattered spiked balls named from the same word to hinder cavalry. Then find the gleam: in the case of the apostates described man is helpless and God's curse is near, but in that very word there is mercy, since the end is not yet come.

Read the similitude as an argument about timing rather than about soil. As the earth cannot bring a good crop at harvest unless it causes the seed to germinate as soon as it is sown, so if we mean to bring forth fruit the word must strike root without delay the moment the Lord sows it, since seed choked or perished cannot fructify; and the ground which sucks in the rain and at once produces a blade suitable to what was sown will by God's blessing go on to a ripe crop. Contrariwise the earth which after culture and irrigation brings forth nothing but thorns affords no hope of a harvest, and the more that grows which is its natural produce, the more hopeless the case. Apply the two soils allegorically as well: the fruitful ground is those who receive the seed of the word, and the thorns and briers stand for errors, heresies and evil works, which show that the seed was never sown in such hearts at all.

Put the emphasis on how the passage should be heard. Let us hear the oracles of God with fear and much trembling, for if even our joy and our exultation ought to be with trembling, of what punishment are we not worthy if we listen without terror to words themselves so fearful. Insist on the source: this threat is not the apostle's and these words are not of man, but of the Holy Ghost and of Christ speaking in him. Then set the sentence in its place, that having said it is impossible for the fallen to be baptized a second time and to receive remission through the laver, and having pointed out the awfulness of the case, he goes on at once to the earth that drinks in the rain.

Quote the Georgics on the custom of burning barren fields, with the rendering about kindled fires burning the barren ground and the light stubble crackling in the wind — and then deny that this is what is meant, since the nature of the case prevents us from supposing an allusion to burning for further fertilisation. What is described instead is land given up as unimprovable, its brushwood burnt off and the ground left to be pastured by the beasts. Read the whole as an argument about husbandry: in giving up such apostates as utterly incurable we act as men do in cultivating their fields, since the ground which drinks the rain brings forth fruit to compensate the toil of the tiller and continues to be cultivated.

debates.question: What does the burning refer to?

sides.position: The common practice among Oriental and Roman farmers of burning bad and barren lands, as Pliny illustrates
Not burning for fertilisation, which the nature of the case forbids, but land given up as unimprovable, its brushwood burnt off and the ground left to pasture
The land God overthrew, which is brimstone and salt and burning

debates.question: Is there mercy in the word nigh?

sides.position: Yes: man is helpless and the curse is near, but in that very word there is mercy, since the end is not yet come
The clause devotes to destruction in the farmer's sense; the land is abandoned as valueless and given over to fire
Timing: the word must strike root the moment it is sown, since seed choked or perished cannot fructify
The consequence of failing to improve privileges — if Christians become like barren earth they will be cast away
How the passage should be heard: with fear and much trembling, since the threat is not the apostle's but the Holy Ghost's

outliers.note: Alone quotes the Georgics on burning barren fields and then denies that this is the practice alluded to, holding that the nature of the case forbids a reference to burning for fertilisation.
Alone reads the similitude as an argument about timing rather than about soil, making the point that the seed must strike root the moment it is sown if there is to be a crop at harvest.

themes: the earth which drinketh in the rain
nigh unto cursing, whose end is to be burned

9.pericope_label: But, beloved, we are persuaded better things of you, and things that accompany salvation, though we thus speak. For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name, in that ye have ministered to the saints, and do minister. And we desire that every one of you do shew the same diligence to the full assurance of hope unto the end: That ye be not slothful, but followers of them who through faith and patience inherit the promises.

schools.summary: Hear the phrase as answering the parable just used: the land overrun with briers was nigh to cursing, while the things seen in these readers were nigh to salvation — the writer has not written in despair but for warning only, believing that what borders on them is not the curse but the alternative. Give two reasons why forgetting their work would be unrighteous, that it was fitting the work be remembered and that reward was expressly promised, while stating the distinction that man's work cannot in itself merit reward but the righteous God cannot neglect his own promise and law that such works shall receive reward. Add the dry qualification that even God cannot remember what they did not do. Report the textual point that the best manuscripts omit the word for labour, so that the clause runs to forget your work, and the love which ye showed toward his name. Notice the difference of tense in the next clause, the same verb appearing first as an aorist and then a present, single act against repeated acts. On the closing exhortation prefer become not sluggish, pointing out that the adjective is the one used earlier of their dullness in apprehending truth and that some were already such; and distinguish the word for patience here from the one used later in the epistle, that being brave endurance and this the term usually rendered long-suffering, which here signifies patient waiting.

Set the two appeals side by side: having applied himself to their fears in order to excite diligence and prevent apostasy, the writer now applies himself to their hopes, freely declaring the good hope he has of them and proposing the encouragements they have in the way of their duty. Then draw the observations out in order — that there are things which accompany salvation, never separated from it, showing the person to be in a state of salvation; that these are better things than any hypocrite or apostate ever enjoyed, better in their nature and in their issue; that it is our duty to hope well of those in whom nothing appears to the contrary; and that ministers must sometimes speak by way of caution even to those of whom they hope the best.

Justify the turn from threat to encouragement as a rule of teaching: the preceding sentences were like thunderbolts by which readers might have been struck dead, so the severity needed mitigating, and whoever wishes to do good by teaching ought so to treat his disciples as to add encouragement rather than diminish it, since nothing alienates us from the truth so much as seeing that we are deemed past hope. Draw the conclusion running the other way too, that not only the reprobate but the elect need reproving severely. Then meet the question of merit head on: the words seem to make God a debtor to human service, and the schoolmen made much of the sentence, concluding that it would be unjust for him not to render eternal salvation as the reward of works — but the apostle is not here speaking of the cause of our salvation, so that no opinion about the merit of works can be formed from the passage. Explain finally why one example is singled out from the many who shared the same faith, since a naked truth does not affect us as much as seeing what is required of us fulfilled in a particular person.

Note that the writer here softens what he had said, commending the good that is in them and exciting them to watchfulness after the most solemn warning against apostasy. Take the things that accompany salvation as things suitable to a state of salvation, and set the readers against their countrymen: several of their brethren have already apostatized and the whole nation is in rebellion, having the things suitable to and indicative of a state of reprobation. On the reward, hold that God is bound to men only by his own promise, which he was not obliged to make, but that once made his justice requires him to keep it — so that God's promise is God's debt. Report that the word for labour before love is wanting in almost every manuscript and version of importance, and that Griesbach left it out of the text. Then make diligence the condition of assurance: slothfulness deprives men of both hope and faith, and it is the faith which works by love that maintains hope in its full exercise.

debates.question: Does the promised reward make God a debtor to works?

sides.position: No: the apostle is not speaking of the cause of salvation, so no opinion about merit can be formed from the passage
God is bound only by his own promise, which he was not obliged to make; but once made, his justice requires him to keep it — God's promise is God's debt
Man's work cannot in itself merit reward, but the righteous God cannot neglect his own promise and law
Forgetting would be unrighteous both because it was fitting the work be remembered and because reward was expressly promised

debates.question: Does the text read work and labour of love?

sides.position: The word for labour is wanting in almost every manuscript of importance and Griesbach left it out
The best manuscripts omit it, so the clause runs your work, and the love which ye showed toward his name

debates.question: Why is the tone changed here?

sides.position: Because whoever teaches ought to add encouragement rather than diminish it, since nothing alienates us like being deemed past hope
Because the writer, having applied himself to their fears, now applies himself to their hopes
Because the phrase answers the parable: the briers were nigh to cursing, these readers nigh to salvation

outliers.note: Alone supplies the limiting qualification to the whole discussion of reward, that even God cannot remember what they did not do.

Alone names the schoolmen as the opponents on this verse and answers them by distinguishing what the passage is about, denying that any opinion on the merit of works can be formed from a sentence not concerned with the cause of salvation.

themes: God is not unrighteous to forget your work
followers of them who through faith and patience inherit

13.pericope_label: For when God made promise to Abraham, because he could swear by no greater, he sware by himself, Saying, Surely blessing I will bless thee, and multiplying I will multiply thee. And so, after he had patiently endured, he obtained the promise.

schools.summary: State the connection as a parallel drawn for the readers: they, like Abraham, have promises to which God has given all possible certainty, and can attain the fulfilment only through faith and patient waiting. Explain why this example rather than another — because he relied on a promise when appearances were against its fulfilment and so shows the advantage of perseverance, and because the assurance given him was confirmed by oath and included the promise of the Christ. Note that the promises made to Abraham were essentially one, with various parts progressively fulfilled, and that although the words quoted come from the account of the offering, the writer probably has earlier promises in mind as well. State the ground of the oath flatly, that there is no being greater than God. Then count the interval: Abraham was seventy-five when called, twenty-four years passed before the manner of the fulfilment was made known, and he was a hundred before it held good. But deny that this is what the verse means by obtaining: though some portions of the promise received a partial accomplishment during Abraham's life, it is not that which the writer has in view.

Explain the strategy of the appeal before its substance. Having boldly reflected on their faults and sufficiently alarmed them, the writer consoles them first by praises and then, on stronger ground, by the assurance that they will certainly attain the object of their hope; and he draws that consolation not from things future but from things past, which will the rather persuade them, since in the matter of punishment he alarms by what is to come and in the matter of prizes he encourages by what has been. Infer from this a divine habit: not to bring in what has been promised immediately but after a long time, both to present the greatest proof of his power and to lead us to faith, so that those living in tribulation without having received the promises or the rewards may not faint under their troubles. Then say why Abraham is brought forward out of the many who might have been mentioned, both for the dignity of his person and for what followed.

Prove that the grace of God is offered in vain unless the promise is received by faith and constantly cherished, and prove it from the improbability of the case: Sarah had been barren through life, both had reached a sterile old age and were nearer the grave than the marriage bed, there was no vigour left to beget children, and who could believe that a nation equalling the stars in number and the sand of the sea would proceed from them? It was contrary to all reason; yet Abraham looked for it and feared no disappointment, because he relied on the word of God, and after waiting twenty-five years a son was given. Take the promise obtained to be the particular thing previously referred to, the numerous posterity.

Supply the occasion: the promise referred to was made when Abraham had offered his son on the altar, and quote the passage in full — that in blessing God would bless him and multiply his seed as the stars of heaven and the sand upon the seashore, and that in his seed all the nations of the earth should be blessed — noting that the apostle quotes only a part, as is generally the case, because he knew his readers were well acquainted with the older Scriptures. Explain what the oath pledged, that God pledged his eternal power and Godhead, there being no superior to whom he could appeal or by whom he could be bound. Then extend the obtaining forward: the supernatural birth of Isaac only began the fulfilment, Abraham saw provision made for the multiplying of his seed, and continuing steadfast in the faith he received the end of all the promises in the enjoyment of an eternal glory — from which draw the inference that if we believe and prove faithful unto death we shall also inherit the promises.

sides.position: For the dignity of his person, and because God's way is to bring in the promise after a long time, so that those in tribulation may not faint
Because the assurance given him was confirmed by oath and included the promise of the Christ
Because he relied on the promise when appearances were against its fulfilment, and so shows the advantage of perseverance
Because though he shared this faith with all the godly, he is the clearest mirror of it and the father of the faithful
The numerous posterity, granted after twenty-five years of waiting
The beginning of it in Isaac, and then the end of all the promises in the enjoyment of an eternal glory
Not the partial accomplishment during his life; that is not what the writer has in view

outliers.note: Alone derives a general habit of God from the delay, that he does not bring in what has been promised immediately but after a long time, both to prove his power and so that those living in tribulation without the promises may not faint.
Alone denies that the obtaining refers to anything accomplished within Abraham’s lifetime, against two who count the years to Isaac’s birth and one who extends it to an eternal glory.

themes: because he could swear by no greater, he sware by himself
surely blessing I will bless thee
after he had patiently endured, he obtained the promise

16.pericope_label: For men verily swear by the greater: and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife. Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath: That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us: Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil; Whither the forerunner is for us entered, even Jesus, made an high priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec.

schools.summary: Bring out the oddity of the construction: when a man confirms a promise by solemn appeal to God, God stands as mediator between the two; here God, condescending to human weakness that the certainty may be more abundant, is at once the promiser and the mediator, so that God the promiser appeals to God the hearer and witness of the oath. Note that the verb is used elsewhere of acting as surety, and that the word for immutability is a late compound meaning unchangeableness of will. On the two immutable things, report the alternatives before choosing: most expositors take them for the promise and the oath, each a firm ground of assurance in which it would be impossible for God to lie, while one refers them instead to two oaths, the one sworn to Abraham and the one by which the Messiah was made high priest after the order of Melchisedec — and object that the apostle seems to refer to two things distinct in their nature rather than to two acts of the same kind. Then take up the anchor: quote the sayings that grounding hope on a false supposition is like trusting to a weak anchor, and that a ship ought not to trust one anchor nor life one hope; note that the symbol is absent from the older Scriptures but current in Greek proverbs and found on ancient coins; and close on the observation that the anchor is out of sight but holds, which is what matters.

Read the oath as an accommodation and then turn it into an argument for assurance. God as a gracious Father accommodates himself to our slowness to believe, and seeing that we do not rest on his simple word he adds an oath to impress it more fully; from which infer how much it concerns us to know that there is such certainty about his goodwill that no occasion for wavering remains. Press the inference from God's own law about swearing: since he forbids his name to be taken on a slight occasion and threatens vengeance on those who abuse it, he holds that name in the highest honour, so that one who forbids men to swear without reason and has yet been pleased to swear himself shows how necessary the certainty of salvation is. Add that the word of God is in itself worthy of trust, pure and without dross like gold seven times purified, so that when an oath is added it is an overplus added to a full measure. Then press the anchor and note where it fails: as long as we sojourn here we stand on no firm ground but are tossed as in a turbulent sea, and the anchor cast through the water into a dark unseen place keeps the beaten vessel from being overwhelmed — but the anchor is cast downwards, having the earth for its bottom, whereas our hope rises upwards and soars aloft, finding nothing in the world to stand on.

Distinguish what each of the two immutable things pledges: the promise pledges faithfulness and justice, the oath all the infinite perfections of the Godhead, for he swore by himself. Quote the rabbinic saying on by thine own self — had God sworn by heaven and earth, one might say that as these pass away so might the oath, but having sworn by his great name which endures for ever, his oath endures for ever. Take the heirs of promise as all the believing posterity of Abraham together with the Gentiles, and the immutable counsel as the unchangeable purpose to call the Gentiles by Jesus Christ, to justify every penitent by faith, and to bring every persevering believer to eternal glory. Then build the anchor into a scene: a vessel nearing port cannot get in over shallow and broken water, so she carries her sheet anchor inside the pier head by means of her boat and rides out the storm at the length of her cable, agitated but not driving, until the tide flows and the crew wear her in against the anchor that has kept its hold.

debates.question: What are the two immutable things?

sides.position: The promise and the oath, as most expositors hold
Two oaths — the one sworn to Abraham and the one making the Messiah high priest after the order of Melchisedec

debates.question: How can God be both promiser and mediator of the oath?

sides.position: By condescension to human weakness: God the promiser appeals to God the hearer and witness
Because he accommodates himself to our slowness to believe, adding an oath to a word already worthy of trust — an overplus added to a full measure

debates.question: How far does the anchor image carry?

sides.position: All the way, in a scene of a vessel riding out the storm on a sheet anchor carried inside the pier head
Not all the way: the anchor is cast downwards to the earth, whereas our hope rises upwards and soars aloft
For a moment only, to set forth the security of a soul tossed by waves; the symbol is absent from the older Scriptures but current in Greek proverbs
Far enough to note that the anchor is out of sight but holds, which is what matters

outliers.note: Alone reports and weighs a rival account of the two immutable things — that they are two oaths, the one to Abraham and the one making the Messiah a priest after the order of Melchisedec — before rejecting it because the apostle seems to mean two things distinct in nature.
Alone marks where the anchor image breaks down, since an anchor is cast downwards and finds bottom in the earth whereas hope rises upwards and finds nothing in the world to stand on.

themes: two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie
an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast
